problem: The sentence is self-contradictory and will be misread. If 95 per cent of the pixels called class A really are A (the diagonal cell), then most of another class has NOT been wrongly assigned to A — that would push the diagonal percentage down. What the trap means to say is the opposite: a class may be 95 per cent correct as a user's view while many of its own true pixels are labelled as another class, so its producer's accuracy is low.
fix: High overall accuracy does not remove class confusion. Read the error matrix by row and column. A class can be 95 per cent correct on the diagonal (user's accuracy) and yet have a low producer's accuracy, because many of its own ground pixels were labelled as another class. Check both directions before trusting any single class.

problem: 'water and cloud are negative' is too strong for cloud. Thick cloud is bright in both red and near-infrared, so its NDVI sits close to zero; only thin or thin-cirrus cloud and some shadowed cloud give clearly negative values. Water is genuinely negative (also snow and shadow).
fix: NDVI runs from −1 to +1; healthy crops approach 0.8, bare soil about 0.2, water and shadow are negative, and thick cloud stays close to zero.

problem: With a 3 × 3 kernel of weight 1/9 the output averages the nine values in the window, including the centre pixel — not 'the nine neighbours', which reads as nine other pixels.
fix: A low-pass kernel gives every cell the weight 1/9; the output is the average of the nine cells in the window, the centre pixel included.

problem: 'Bilinear interpolation averages four neighbours' hides the weighting. The four neighbours are weighted by distance from the output point, which is why the result is smoother than nearest neighbour.
fix: Bilinear interpolation takes the four nearest input pixels and averages them with weights that fall with distance, so the result looks smoother but invents new DN values.
